messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 44

Dr. Mendez was driving home after a twelve-hour shift when the other car ran a red light. He remembers the headlights growing—not the sound of impact, but the split-second thought that his hands were about to be destroyed. A surgeon’s hands. He had spent thirty years in the operating room, repairing what others broke, and now he was the one bleeding on the asphalt. The paramedics had to cut his wedding ring off. That detail comes back to him most nights, just before he wakes up.

In the months since the accident, he has not spoken about it. Not to his wife, not to his colleagues. When residents ask about the limp, he says “old sports injury.” But his body tells a different story. He still drives, but his knuckles are white the whole way. He takes surface streets only, avoids intersections with traffic lights, and always leaves the hospital an hour early to avoid rush hour. The hospital’s parking garage feels like a cage; he walks to his car with his keys pressed between his fingers, scanning every shadow. He knows it is irrational. He tells himself that during morning rounds. By noon, he is checking the exit routes in the OR again.

The worst moments happen when he is scrubbing in. The smell of antiseptic soap—that sharp, chemical clean—triggers a vivid image of the EMT wiping blood from his face. His pulse spikes. His hands tremble for a second before he forces them steady. He has learned to pause, to take a breath, but the tremor is a secret he cannot afford. In the operating room, a shaky hand can kill. So he has started avoiding the most complex cases. He tells the chief he is “easing back.” The chief trusts him. Dr. Mendez has never lied before.

At home, he is irritable. His wife thinks he is depressed. He snaps at her for leaving the garage light on—the brightness reminds him of the headlights. He has stopped sitting in the living room armchair that faces the window; he says the light bothers his eyes. The truth is, he cannot bear the vulnerability of not seeing what is coming. He has begun sleeping in the guest room because his wife’s breathing—soft and rhythmic—makes him feel trapped, like he is in the wreckage. He lies awake, his wife’s wedding band on his own pinky finger (his had to be cut), tracing the scar across his palm with his thumb. He replays the accident frame by frame, looking for the split decision that could have saved him.

He has not cried. He has not told anyone about the nightmares. In the morning, he drinks black coffee and reads the obituaries. He does not know why. He just keeps expecting to see his own name.
